item.title: The opener buys the room, not the laugh
item.description:
Twenty years of walking into cold rooms and I'll say the unpopular thing: your opener's job isn't to be your funniest joke. Its job is to answer the only question the audience is silently asking — "are we in good hands?" Get that yes, and they'll ride with you.
Scar tissue, catalogued: - **The masterpiece opener**: leading with your best, most layered bit before the room trusts you. I've bombed with material that killed twenty minutes deep in other sets, because a cold room won't do the work a warm one will. Fix: open with something short, sturdy, and crowd-proof — save the cathedral for after they've bought a ticket. - **The apology walk-on**: opening with "I just wrote this" or fiddling with the mic stand for eight seconds of dead air. The room reads nerves faster than words. Fix: the first ten seconds are choreography — planted feet, first line loaded, no preamble. - **The borrowed-energy trap**: matching a hype host's frantic energy when your act is dry and slow. You spend the whole set as someone else. I've watched comics burn their first five minutes impersonating the intro. item.title: Hydration is a schedule, not a sensation
item.description:
Two decades of coaching and the clients who fade in the last third of a session are rarely under-fueled — they're under-watered and waiting for thirst to tell them. By the time thirst shows up, you're already behind, and behind is where lifts get ugly.
Failure modes I see on repeat: - **The camel strategy**: nothing all day, then a liter chugged in the parking lot before training. I've watched people cramp mid-set and blame electrolytes when the real issue was showing up dry and trying to fix it in ten minutes. Fix: water rides along with meals and transitions — sip on a schedule the body can actually absorb. - **The coffee accounting error**: counting three espressos and a pre-workout as fluid intake. The math feels right and the afternoon headache disagrees. Fix: caffeine drinks are neutral at best — they don't earn hydration credit, they just don't cost much. - **The clear-urine trophy hunt**: overcorrecting into constant chugging, flushing electrolytes, feeling sloshy and weirdly flat. More is not the fix; timing is. Fix: pale yellow is the target, and salt your food like an adult who sweats.

item.title: Avoidance pays interest daily
item.description:
Two decades across the table and the most expensive habit I've watched isn't rage or panic — it's the unopened envelope. The email not replied to, the scan not booked, the conversation postponed until it calcifies. Avoidance always feels like a loan with no payments due. It isn't. It compounds while you sleep.
Failure modes I've watched play out: - **The relief trap**: dodging the hard thing produces instant calm, and the brain files that relief as evidence the dodge worked. I've watched people build entire routines around never touching one folder. Fix: name the mechanism out loud — "this calm is the drug, not the solution" — because a labeled trap catches fewer feet. - **The threat inflation spiral**: the longer a task is avoided, the bigger it grows in imagination. A two-line reply becomes a confrontation, becomes a catastrophe. The task never changed; the story did. Fix: write down what the task actually requires in physical steps. Paper shrinks what imagination inflates. - **The perfect-conditions alibi**: "I'll deal with it when things settle down." I've watched that sentence hold for years. Conditions never settle; they rotate. Fix: attach the avoided thing

item.title: A runbook nobody rehearses is a novel
item.description:
Twenty years of incidents and I've stopped counting the 2am pages where the runbook existed, was beautifully formatted, and was wrong in the third step. A runbook that's never been executed under pressure isn't documentation — it's fiction with headers.
Named failure modes I've paid for: - **The stale credential step**: "log into the admin console" — with an account that was deprovisioned two quarters ago. I've watched an outage stretch forty minutes while we hunted for anyone who still had access. Fix: every runbook step that touches auth gets exercised in the quarterly game day, by the newest person on the team, not the author. - **The tribal-knowledge gap**: step four says "restart the service" and assumes you know which of the six systemd units is *the* service. The author knew. The author is on a plane. Fix: runbooks are written for the person who has never seen the system — exact commands, exact hostnames, copy-pasteable. - **The happy-path runbook**: it covers the restart but not what to do when the restart hangs, which is the only time you'd be reading it. item.title: Sleep debt doesn't forgive — it refinances
item.description:
I've coached people for two decades who treated sleep like a credit line: borrow all week, repay Saturday. I've watched that ledger from the training floor — the repayment never clears the balance, it just rolls the interest forward into their lifts, their mood, and their injuries.
Named failure modes I've watched wreck progress:
- **The weekend binge repay.** Five short nights, then eleven hours Saturday. The circadian whiplash means Monday feels like jet lag, and the training week starts in a hole again. - **The caffeine refinance.** The debt gets serviced with a second and third coffee, which pushes bedtime later, which deepens the debt. It's a payday loan with a nicer smell. - **The "I'm fine" adaptation.** After a couple of weeks of short sleep, people stop feeling tired — but I've watched their bar speed, their reaction time, and their patience with their kids all say otherwise. You adapt to the feeling, not the deficit. - **The heavy day collision.** The week's worst night somehow always lands before the heaviest session, because both were scheduled around the same overloaded life. That's where tweaks and misses come from.

item.title: Reassurance-seeking is scratching a bite — it spreads the itch
item.description:
Twenty years of sitting with anxious minds and I've watched the same trade happen thousands of times: a moment of relief purchased now, paid for with a bigger dose of doubt tomorrow. Reassurance works — that's exactly the problem. It works like scratching works.
Named failure modes I've watched people cycle through:
- **The escalating dose.** "Are we okay?" once a month becomes once a week becomes nightly. The reassurance still lands, but the half-life shrinks every time, and the asker feels crazier, not calmer. - **The outsourced certainty.** The person stops consulting their own judgment entirely. Every decision gets pre-cleared with a partner, a friend, a search bar. The muscle that tolerates not-knowing atrophies from disuse. - **The reassurer's burnout.** The partner who lovingly answers every "are you sure?" is training the loop while slowly resenting it. I've watched relationships buckle not from the anxiety but from the reassurance economy built around it. - **The disguised check.** It stops looking like a question — it becomes rereading the sent email, re-checking the lock, scanning their face at dinner. item.title: Crowd work is a detour, not a destination
item.description:
I've bombed enough rooms over twenty years to know the seduction: crowd work gets the fastest laughs in the building, so young comics start treating it as the act. I've watched killers-in-the-room become nobodies-on-tape because nothing they did could survive outside that one Tuesday.
Named failure modes I've paid for on stage:
- **The rented laugh.** The bit belongs to the drunk dentist in row two. It dies the second he leaves. You built nothing you can use tomorrow. - **The escape hatch habit.** Every time a written joke wobbles, you bail into "where are you from?" — and your material never gets the reps it needs to get good, because you never let it fail long enough to fix it. - **The hostage interview.** You mistake interrogating a shy table for engagement. The room isn't laughing with you, it's relieved you haven't picked them. That tension reads as energy from the stage and reads as cruelty on tape. - **The tape that can't travel.** The booker asks for a clip and everything killer you have is fifteen minutes of local references and one guy's divorce. Nothing submits, nothing books.

item.title: An on-call rotation without a handoff is a relay with no baton
item.description:
I've watched an incident burn for six extra hours because the outgoing on-call knew exactly what was smoldering and the incoming one found out from the pager. Twenty years of rotations and the pattern never changes: the schedule tool is immaculate, the handoff is a shrug in Slack.
Named failure modes I've eaten:
- **The silent smolder.** Outgoing engineer watched a queue depth creep all week, decided it "wasn't page-worthy yet," and told nobody. It became page-worthy at 3am on the new person's first night. - **The tribal runbook.** The fix lives in one person's head — "oh you just restart the consumer with the flag" — and that person is now on a plane. The written runbook was last touched two reorgs ago. - **The mute inheritance.** Previous on-call muted a flapping alert to survive their week and never unmuted it. The next real incident of that class fired into a black hole. - **The context cliff.** A risky deploy shipped Friday afternoon; the weekend on-call didn't know it existed. Every symptom got debugged from zero instead of from "what changed."

item.title: The callback is a gift you set up before you give it
item.description:
I've bombed with a callback that should have crushed, purely because I never planted the seed cleanly the first time. A callback isn't a joke you find at the end — it's a promise you made in the first two minutes and forgot to keep with intent.
Failure modes I've watched newer comics fall into:
- **The un-planted callback.** They reference an earlier bit that the audience only half-registered, because the setup line was mumbled or buried. You can't call back a thing the room never locked in. Plant it loud, then move on like it was nothing. - **The too-soon callback.** They fire it ninety seconds after the original. That's not a callback, that's a repeat — the audience hasn't had time to forget, so there's no surprise to reward. - **The over-milked callback.** It hits, so they run it a fourth and fifth time. The third callback is where laughter turns to a polite exhale. I've watched a killer tag die of overuse in real time. - **The callback that needs a footnote.** If you have to remind them what you're referencing, the joke is already dead. item.title: Protein is the floor, not the ceiling, of a diet
item.description:
I've coached people who tracked every macro to the gram and still lost muscle on a cut, because they treated protein as the thing to minimize around everything else. Backwards. Protein is the number you hit FIRST and build the rest of the plate around.
Failure modes I've watched trap people:
- **The last-slot protein.** They fill up on carbs and fat, then squeeze in whatever protein fits the calorie budget. On a deficit that means chronically under-eating it, and the scale drops because muscle is leaving, not just fat. - **The single-dose day.** All their protein in one giant dinner. The body can only do so much with one massive bolus; spreading it across the day does far more for holding muscle than one heroic steak. - **The "clean" trap.** They chase only whole-food protein and fall short every day because chicken and eggs alone are hard to hit volume with. A shake isn't cheating; it's a tool that closes the gap when appetite or time won't. - **The plant hand-wave.** Going plant-based and assuming beans "count" the same. item.title: Comparison is a tax you volunteer to pay
item.description:
I've watched capable people stall for years, not from lack of skill but from measuring their raw footage against everyone else's highlight reel. Comparison isn't information — it's a tax on attention you keep choosing to pay, and it never funds anything you can use.
Failure modes I've watched trap people (myself first):
- **The reel-vs-footage error.** They compare their behind-the-scenes mess to someone's published, edited, curated output. Of course they come up short — they're comparing two different categories and calling it a verdict. - **The moving goalpost.** They hit the milestone they envied, feel nothing, and instantly find a new person one rung up to feel behind. The comparison engine doesn't want a destination; it wants fuel, and it will always find more. - **The wrong-axis compare.** They measure themselves on someone else's strength while ignoring the tradeoffs that person made to get it. You're seeing the win, not the marriage or the health or the years it cost. - **The proximity trap.** The comparisons that hurt most aren't celebrities — they're the peer one desk over. item.title: A dependency you don't pin is a deploy you don't control
item.description:
I've watched a green build turn red overnight with not one line of our code changed. A transitive dep shipped a patch release, our unpinned range pulled it, and a Friday deploy became a Saturday incident. "It's just a patch bump" is the most expensive sentence in software.
Named failure modes I've eaten:
- **The floating range.** A caret or tilde range that silently pulls a new minor the moment upstream publishes. Your lockfile said one thing, your CI runner resolved another, and now "works on my machine" is literally true and useless. - **The phantom transitive.** You pinned your direct deps and felt safe, but a dep-of-a-dep floated freely underneath. The breaking change came from a package you've never heard of and can't grep for. - **The lockfile nobody commits.** The team pins in theory but the lock file is gitignored "because it's noisy in diffs." Every developer and every CI run resolves a slightly different tree. item.title: Punching up is a compass, not a cage
item.description:
I've watched rooms go cold in a way that has nothing to do with the joke's craft and everything to do with who it lands on. The mechanics were clean; the target was wrong. The audience wasn't offended — they just decided you were the bully, and nobody laughs at a bully.
Named failure modes from years of eating silence:
- **The easy target.** Aiming at whoever's already down. The room senses the cheapness instantly; it reads as cruelty wearing a joke costume. - **The self-deprecation overdose.** Punching so far down at yourself that the audience stops finding it brave and starts finding it sad. There's a line where humble becomes a wound you're making them watch. - **The inside-baseball miss.** A joke that only punches if you already know the target. Half the room can't tell who you're hitting, so it reads as random aggression. - **The stale target.** Beating a subject the culture already resolved. You're not brave, you're late, and lateness in comedy reads as out of touch. - **The mismatched room.** A perfectly aimed bit that hits a nerve THIS specific crowd is still raw about. Same words, wrong room, dead air.

item.title: Motivation follows action, it doesn't lead it
item.description:
I wasted years waiting to feel ready. I treated motivation like weather — something that arrives on its own and lets you work once it shows up. It doesn't. In practice, the feeling shows up AFTER you start, not before. Waiting for it is waiting for a bus that only comes once you're already walking.
Named failure modes I've watched trap people (myself first):
- **The readiness trap.** "I'll start when I feel like it." The feeling is downstream of starting, so you've built a loop that never fires. - **The all-or-nothing start.** Refusing to begin unless you can do the full thing perfectly. The bar is so high the first step never happens, and no step means no momentum to ride. - **The mood-as-verdict error.** Reading low motivation as proof the goal is wrong. Low energy is a state, not a message about your values. - **The dopamine-substitute.** Scrolling or planning to feel the SENSATION of progress without the cost of it. It scratches the itch just enough to kill the real start. - **The identity delay.** Waiting to "become the kind of person who does this" before doing it. Backwards — you become that person by doing the thing badly, repeatedly, first.

item.title: Mobility is strength you can actually reach
item.description:
I spent years chasing bigger numbers while my range of motion quietly shrank. Then a shoulder that couldn't get overhead cleanly turned a heavy press into a slow-motion injury. Strength you can't express through a full range is just a liability with good marketing.
Named failure modes I've watched wreck people:
- **The half-rep hero.** Loads huge, moves an inch. Builds strength only in the range he already owns and none in the range that keeps him safe when he slips. - **The static-stretch-before-lifting mistake.** Long passive holds right before heavy work leave the muscle sleepy and slow to fire. Save the long holds for after; warm up with movement, not with sitting in a stretch. - **The mobility-as-punishment trap.** Treats mobility as ten miserable minutes of penance instead of loaded, controlled reps through end range — which is the only version that actually sticks. - **The tight-equals-strong myth.** A joint that won't move isn't stable, it's braced. Bracing is a cost, not a strength; it borrows against the joint above and below. - **The symmetry blind spot.** Trains both sides with the same load while one side quietly does the work. item.title: A feature flag you never remove becomes a second codebase
item.description:
I've shipped flags that outlived the feature they gated by years. Nobody deletes them because nobody's sure who's still on the old path. That's how you end up maintaining two products with one team.
Named failure modes I've eaten:
- **The zombie flag.** Feature fully rolled out, flag still branching in the hot path. Every reader now has to reason about a dead `else` that can never run — until someone "cleans it up" and discovers a cron in another service still flips it. - **The nested flag.** Flag inside a flag inside a flag. The combinatorics mean you have paths in production that no human has ever exercised. Your test matrix quietly gave up three flags ago. - **The config-as-flag.** Someone turned a permanent business rule into a runtime toggle "for flexibility." Now product behavior lives in a dashboard nobody version-controls, and your incident postmortem has no diff to point at. - **The kill-switch nobody tested.** The flag that's supposed to save you in an outage has never been flipped under load. item.title: Sleep is where you actually get stronger — the workout is just the stimulus
item.description:
Two decades of coaching and the plateau I've untangled most often isn't a programming problem — it's a sleep problem wearing a programming costume. The lifter swears the plan is broken. The plan is fine. They're trying to adapt to a stimulus on five hours a night, and the body simply files the request under "later."
Failure modes I see on repeat: - **Chasing more volume to fix stalled recovery.** Adding sets to a body that isn't recovering from the sets it already has. I've watched strong people dig themselves deeper by "working harder" when the fix was going to bed. Fix: when progress stalls, audit sleep before you touch the program. - **The weekend catch-up myth.** Sleeping four hours short all week and binging ten on Saturday, then wondering why Monday feels like moving through wet sand. Fix: consistency beats totals — a regular window beats a heroic weekend recovery. - **Caffeine masking the debt.** Using stimulants to feel trained-through-tired, so you never notice you're accumulating a deficit until form breaks or something tweaks. item.title: Silence is a tool — the panic to fill it is what kills the joke
item.description:
Twenty years of sets and the tell that separates an open-miker from a headliner isn't the material — it's what they do in the two seconds after a line. The new comic hears silence and sprints. The seasoned one lets it sit, because the pause is where the room decides to laugh.
Scar tissue, catalogued: - **Stepping on the laugh.** Rushing into the next line before the last one landed, so the crowd never gets room to react and learns to stay quiet. I've watched a killer joke die because the comic talked over its own applause break. Fix: say the punchline, then shut up — let the room fill the silence. - **Filling the pause with "anyway…".** Treating every beat of quiet as failure and papering over it with filler, which tells the room the bit didn't work even when it did. Fix: hold the eye contact, trust the beat; confidence in the silence reads as control. - **No pause before the tag.** Firing the callback instantly instead of letting anticipation build, so the tag lands flat instead of detonating. item.title: A boundary is a thing you enforce — not a speech you deliver
item.description:
Two decades across the table from people trying to protect themselves, and the most common heartbreak is watching someone give a beautiful, articulate boundary speech and then abandon it the moment it's tested. A boundary announced but not enforced isn't a boundary — it's a wish you said out loud.
Failure modes I've watched play out: - **The ultimatum you won't keep.** "If you do that again, I'm leaving" — said for the fifth time, still there. I've watched people teach the exact behavior they hate by threatening a consequence they never deliver. Fix: only state a boundary you're actually willing to enforce, then enforce it the first time, quietly. - **Boundary as control.** Trying to use "my boundary" to dictate what the other person does, when a boundary only ever governs what YOU do in response. Fix: frame it as your action ("I'll leave the room if this continues"), not their obligation. - **Over-explaining to earn permission.** Delivering a ten-minute justification because part of you needs the other person to agree it's fair. item.title: A log line nobody reads is just disk you pay to fill
item.description:
Twenty years of shipping backends and the most expensive silence I've lived through wasn't a missing log — it was ten thousand log lines a second that nobody could search when it mattered. We had everything. At 3am, during the incident, we had nothing usable. Volume is not observability.
Named failure modes I've paid for: - **Log-everything-at-INFO.** Every request logs a paragraph, so the one ERROR that matters is buried under a million heartbeats. I've watched an on-call grep for twenty minutes to find a stack trace that was right there. Fix: log at the level that matches the reader's urgency, and make ERROR mean "wake someone." - **Unstructured string soup.** Human-readable prose that no query engine can filter, so you can't ask "show me all failures for this user." Fix: structured logs (key=value or JSON), every line, from day one. - **No correlation ID.** A request fans out to six services and you can't stitch its journey back together. item.title: Willpower is a battery, not a personality trait
item.description:
Twenty years of coaching people through behavior change taught me the most damaging myth in the room: that discipline is a character you either have or lack. I've watched conscientious, capable people flog themselves for "having no willpower" at 9pm — when the real problem is they spent the whole battery by noon and built no system to run on empty.
Named failure modes I've watched people repeat: - **Treating willpower as identity.** "I'm just not disciplined," said as a fixed trait. It becomes a self-fulfilling excuse. Fix: reframe it as a depletable resource — then you manage it instead of grading it. - **Deciding on empty.** Leaving hard choices for the end of the day when the battery is flat. That's when everyone caves. Fix: front-load hard decisions to the morning; automate or pre-commit the evening ones. - **Relying on motivation.** Waiting to feel like it. The feeling is a passenger, not the engine. Fix: build a cue-and-default so the behavior fires without a vote each time. - **White-knuckling temptation.** Keeping the donuts in the house and "resisting." Every glance spends charge. item.title: The straight line is where the audience relaxes so the punchline can land
item.description:
Twenty years of working rooms taught me that new comics obsess over jokes and starve the straight lines — and then wonder why the jokes die. The straight line isn't filler. It's the flat runway the audience needs before you can pull the wheels up. No runway, no takeoff.
Named failure modes I've bombed my way through: - **All punch, no setup.** Cramming a laugh into every line so nothing lands, because the room never gets a beat to breathe. Fix: earn the laugh with a genuine, un-funny setup line — flat is a feature. - **Telegraphing.** Grinning or shifting your voice right before the punchline so they see it coming. Fix: deliver the setup completely straight; let the turn surprise them. - **Stepping on the laugh.** Talking over the laugh you just got, killing it early to rush to the next bit. Fix: shut up and hold — ride the laugh to its peak, then go. - **No point of view in the setup.** Setups that are just facts with no attitude, so the punchline has nothing to subvert. Fix: plant your angle early so the twist has something to break. - **Same rhythm every time.** Setup-punch, setup-punch, metronomic, so the room predicts you. item.title: Grip is the strength that quietly caps every other lift
item.description:
Twenty years under the bar and rehabbing my own cranky forearms taught me that grip is the silent ceiling nobody trains until it fails them. I've watched strong people miss deadlifts not because their back gave out but because the bar rolled out of their hands at rep four — the posterior chain had more to give, the hands didn't.
Named failure modes I've watched cap people: - **Straps for everything.** Living in lifting straps so grip never gets the stimulus, then wondering why a suitcase feels heavy. Fix: strap the top-end heavy sets, but pull your warmups and back-offs raw. - **Only training crush.** Squeezing grippers and ignoring that grip has three jobs — crush, pinch, and support (holding a heavy bar for time). Fix: train all three; support grip is the one that carries deadlifts and carries. - **No carries.** Never doing loaded carries, which are the cheapest grip-and-core builder there is. Fix: farmer's walks or suitcase carries twice a week, heavy and slow. - **Ignoring the elbow.** Hammering grip volume until the inner or outer elbow flares, then quitting entirely. item.title: A retry without a budget is a denial-of-service you wrote yourself
item.description:
Two decades of shipping backend systems taught me that the outage that hurts most is rarely the one the vendor caused — it's the one your own retry loop amplified. I've watched a single flaky downstream turn into a full-region brownout because every caller retried instantly, three times, forever. The dependency blinked; our retry storm is what actually knocked it over.
Named failure modes I've paid for: - **Retries with no cap.** Retrying "until it works" means retrying a dead service into the ground. Fix: bound every retry with a max attempt count AND a total time budget — whichever trips first, you stop. - **No jitter.** Everyone retries on the same 1s/2s/4s schedule, so the herd hits the recovering service in perfect lockstep and re-kills it. Fix: exponential backoff with full jitter, always. - **Retrying non-idempotent writes.** Retrying a POST that already succeeded but timed out on the response — now you've double-charged someone. Fix: idempotency keys, or don't retry writes at all. - **Retrying at every layer.** Client retries 3x, gateway retries 3x, service retries 3x — that's 27 real calls per "one" request. Fix: retry at exactly one layer; everyone else fails fast. - **N

item.title: The callback is a debt you set up earlier
item.description:
Twenty years of writing and bombing taught me a callback isn't a clever afterthought — it's a debt you took out in the first two minutes and repaid at the end with interest. When it lands it feels like magic to the room; backstage you know it was accounting.
Named failure modes I've eaten on stage: - **The callback to nothing.** You reference a bit you never actually planted, so the room hears a punchline shape with no setup underneath and just stares. Fix: plant the reference clearly and early, even if it looks throwaway — no deposit, no withdrawal. - **The over-planted callback.** You lean on the reference so hard the first time that the return feels obligatory, not surprising. Fix: plant it light, almost tossed away, so the return recontextualizes instead of repeats. - **The stale callback.** Too long between setup and payoff and the room has moved on; you're repaying a debt they forgot they held. Fix: mind the gap — a callback has a half-life, close it before the memory decays. - **The identical callback.** Returning the exact same line instead of a twisted version. Repetition is recognition, not a laugh. Fix: change the angle on the return so it rhymes with the setup instead

item.title: Soreness is feedback, not a scoreboard
item.description:
Two decades of training people and rebuilding my own beaten-up joints taught me that the people who chase soreness are usually the ones who plateau, and the ones who quietly show up plateau least. Soreness tells you a stimulus was novel. It does not tell you the session was good, and it definitely doesn't measure progress.
Named failure modes I've watched wreck people: - **Soreness-chasing.** Judging a workout by how wrecked you feel tomorrow. You just reward novelty and punish consistency — the sorest sessions are often the least repeatable. Fix: judge by whether you can add a rep or a little load next time, not by how much you limp. - **The redline every session.** Grinding to failure daily so every day feels heroic. Recovery never catches up and the small tweak becomes the six-week layoff. Fix: leave a couple reps in reserve most days; earn the redline occasionally. - **Ignoring the sharp signal.** Treating a bright, local, joint-line pain like ordinary muscle soreness. That's the one that becomes surgery. Fix: dull and spread-out is soreness; sharp and pinpoint is a stop sign — respect the difference. - **No baseline.** Not logging anything, so you can't tell adaptation from a

item.title: Certainty is a feeling, not a verdict
item.description:
Twenty years sitting across from people untangling their own decisions taught me that certainty is an emotion the brain generates, not a measurement of how true something is. It arrives before the evidence is in and it feels exactly the same whether you're right or catastrophically wrong. That symmetry is the whole problem.
Named failure modes I've watched play out again and again: - **Mistaking fluency for truth.** A story that comes to mind easily feels true because it's smooth, not because it's accurate. Fix: notice when a conclusion arrived too fast — speed is a red flag, not a green one. - **Confidence as a loyalty test.** Doubling down because backing off feels like weakness. The certainty is defending your ego, not your position. item.title: Silence Is a Punchline You Have to Earn
item.description:

**Stepping on the laugh.** The joke lands, the room starts to go, and the comic rushes into the next line — killing the laugh they just built. You have to hold, let the wave crest, and ride it out. Double death. - **The over-signposted return.** "Remember what I said earlier about my landlord?" No. Nobody's holding your set list. The moment you have to explain the setup, the payoff is already dead on arrival. - **The callback with no new information.** Repeating the exact line isn't a callback, it's a rerun. The laugh comes from the same premise arriving in a new, worse situation — escalation, not echo.
The fix: only call back to something that already killed, deploy it when the audience least expects it, and make the return raise the stakes. The best callbacks feel like the universe rhyming, not like the comic filing paperwork.

item.title: Tempo is the variable nobody logs
item.description:
Two decades coaching lifters and the number one hidden cheat isn't load or reps — it's tempo. People add weight, keep the rep count, and quietly shave a full second off the eccentric until they're basically dropping the bar and calling it a set.
Named failure modes I've watched wreck progress:
- **The bounce-rep plateau.** Bench "goes up" for a month because the lifter is using the ribcage as a trampoline. Take the bounce away and they're weaker than they were in week one. You trained elastic recoil, not muscle. - **The ego eccentric.** Loading a weight you can lower but not control. The set looks heavy, the joints eat all of it, and the tendon complains three weeks later when it's too late to blame the obvious cause. - **The invisible regression.** Same weight, same reps in the log, so the log says "maintaining." But the time-under-tension quietly collapsed as fatigue crept in. The paper trail lies because it never recorded the one thing that changed.
The fix: pick a tempo and actually count it — a 3-second lower is a coaching cue you can enforce, not a vibe. When you want to progress without adding load, slow the eccentric first. It's free overload and it's the safest kind.

item.description:
Twenty years of on-call and the healthchecks that fooled me longest were the ones that returned 200 because the web server was up — while the database it needed was face-down in the mud. Green dashboard, dead product.
Named failure modes I've paid for:

item.title: COMEDY — Silence is a punchline you have to trust (20-yr standup voice)
item.description:
**Hook:** Twenty years on stages, and the joke that dies most often isn't the weak one — it's the good one the comic panicked over and stepped on.
**Body:** Here's the scar: you land a line, the room needs a half-second to arrive, and in that half-second the amateur in you fills the gap with "you know?" or a nervous repeat. You just taught the crowd the joke wasn't finished. The laugh was coming; you interrupted it to ask for it.
Named failure modes from a thousand rooms. One: the rush-off — you bail on the beat before the tag lands because silence feels like death. Two: the over-explain — you clarify a joke that landed fine, which reads as "I don't trust you got it." Three: the apology laugh — you laugh at your own line to signal it was a joke, and now you're the only one laughing.
The craft move is nerve, not material: say the line, shut up, hold eye contact, let the silence do the pulling. The best comics aren't the fastest — they're the ones comfortable in the pause.

item.title: TECH — Observability is not monitoring (20-yr distributed-systems voice)
item.description:
**Hook:** After twenty years on call, I can tell you monitoring answers "is it down?" — observability answers "why is it weird?" — and most teams pay for the first while begging for the second.
**Body:** The scar that taught me: a payments service passing every health check while a fraction of users silently got double-charged. Monitoring was green because the endpoint returned two-hundred. Nobody could ask "show me every request where the charge fired twice" because we logged counts, not events with correlation IDs. That's the whole difference — monitoring is pre-decided questions; observability is being able to ask a question you didn't anticipate.
Three failure modes I've watched sink teams. One: cardinality panic — they strip user and request IDs from metrics to save cost, then can't trace a single journey. Two: dashboard theater — twelve screens nobody reads, zero traces. Three: logs as a landfill — everything at INFO, so the one line that matters drowns.
The fix isn't a bigger vendor bill. It's structured events with a correlation ID threaded end to end, sampled smart, queryable after the fact.

item.title: HEALTH — Grip strength is the tell (20-yr strength-coach voice)
item.description:
**Hook:** Twenty years coaching lifters and gen-pop, and the number I trust most isn't bodyweight or a lift max — it's how long you can hang from a bar.
**Body:** Grip is the honest broker. You can grind a bad deadlift with hips and ego; you cannot fake a dead hang. When someone tells me they're "getting stronger" but their hang time is falling, I know what's actually happening — they're training their favorite lifts and neglecting the connective tissue that carries everything else.
Failure modes I see on repeat. One: straps too early — beginners strap up to chase deadlift numbers and their grip never catches up, so the whole chain has a weak link they've hidden. Two: no hanging at all — people treat the bar as a pulling tool, never a loading tool for the hands and shoulders. Three: chasing soreness instead of capacity — a hand that's sore isn't a hand that's stronger.
The intervention is boring and it works: add unstrapped holds and dead hangs, track the seconds, let grip set the ceiling on your pulls instead of hiding under straps.
**CTA:** Time an unstrapped dead hang today. That number, tracked monthly, tells you more than the scale.

item.title: PSYCHOLOGY — Anger is almost always the second thing you felt (20-yr clinician voice)
item.description:
**Hook:** Two decades in the room with people, and I've learned anger is rarely the origin — it's the bodyguard for a softer feeling that showed up first.
**Body:** The pattern is reliable: someone snaps, and underneath the snap, a half-second earlier, was hurt, fear, or shame that felt too exposed to sit with. Anger is metabolically cheaper — it points outward, it feels powerful, it protects. So the mind reaches for it fast. The person isn't lying when they say "I'm just angry." They genuinely can't see the thing anger arrived to cover.
Failure modes I watch people run. One: venting the anger and calling it processing — it rehearses the arousal, it doesn't touch the primary feeling. Two: attacking the anger as the problem — "I need to control my temper" — which fights the bodyguard and never asks who it's guarding. Three: assuming the trigger is the cause — the person who cut you off in traffic didn't create the disproportionate rage; they released it.
The move is to get curious backward: what did I feel one beat before the anger? That's the feeling that actually needs attention.

item.title: The pain is always real — the story about the pain often isn't
item.description:
Two decades across the table from hurting people and the distinction that unlocks the most progress is also the hardest to hear: your feeling is valid, and your explanation for it can still be flat wrong. Those two things live together, and confusing them keeps people stuck.
Failure modes I've watched play out: - **Feeling equals fact**: "I feel disrespected, so they disrespected me." The hurt is real; the intent you assigned may be invented. I've watched people end good relationships over a motive that only ever existed in their own head. Fix: separate "what happened" from "what I told myself it meant" — write both columns and notice how thin the second one is. - **Weaponized validation**: taking "your feelings are valid" to mean "therefore my reading of the situation is correct." Validation is about the feeling, never the interpretation. - **The first story wins**: the earliest explanation your brain reaches for feels like truth because it came fast, not because it's accurate. Speed isn't evidence. Fix: generate a second and third possible explanation before you commit to the first.

item.title: Your warmup isn't a toll you pay — it's the first rep of the workout
item.description:
Two decades of coaching and the lifters who get hurt aren't the reckless ones — they're the ones who treat the warmup as wasted time to rush through so the "real" work can start. The warmup IS real work. It's where you find out what today's body actually has.
Failure modes I see on repeat: - **The cold heavy single**: skipping ramp-up sets to "save energy," then wondering why the first heavy rep felt like a stranger's body. I've watched strong people tweak a back on a weight they own, purely because they arrived cold. Fix: ramp in real jumps — the ramp tells you today's ceiling before it costs you. - **Static-stretch-and-go**: long passive stretches right before heavy loading, then loading a muscle you just told to relax. Fix: warm up by moving through the pattern you're about to train, under light load, not by holding still. - **Ignoring the readout**: the warmup felt awful and you bulldozed into the top set anyway. The warmup was the data; you deleted it. Fix: if the ramp feels wrong, that's the workout telling you to deload today, not push.

item.title: A metric you don't alert on is a diary entry, not monitoring
item.description:
Twenty years in and the postmortem line I've written most is some variant of "the dashboard showed it the whole time." We had the graph. Nobody was looking at 3am. A metric with no alert is a diary you read after the funeral.
Named failure modes I've paid for: - **The vanity dashboard**: forty panels, all green, and the one that mattered was three scrolls down with no threshold on it. I've watched an on-call stare at a wall of graphs and still miss the SLO burn. Fix: every panel that can page you should page you; the rest belong in a report, not on the war-room screen. - **Alerting on causes instead of symptoms**: paging on "CPU pegged" when the user impact is "checkout latency doubled." You get woken for noise and sleep through the outage. Fix: alert on the symptom your user feels, then use the cause metrics to debug. - **The alert nobody trusts**: it fires so often on nothing that the team mutes it, and then it's decorative. I've seen a real incident ignored because "that thing always cries wolf." Fix: if an alert isn't actionable every time, it's a bug — fix or delete it.

item.title: A heckler hands you the room — if you stop trying to win the argument
item.description:
Twenty years of sets and the newest comics all make the same mistake with a heckler: they try to be RIGHT. The room doesn't want right. The room wants to see who's in control. The second you argue, you've handed them the wheel.
Scar tissue, catalogued: - **Debating the heckler**: matching their logic point for point, which turns a comedy show into a losing courtroom. I've watched a strong set die because the comic "won" the argument and lost the crowd. Fix: don't out-reason them, re-frame them — you control the mic, use it. - **The canned put-down on a live line**: firing a memorized crushback that doesn't fit what they actually said, so it reads as defensive, not sharp. Fix: react to the specific thing; specificity is what the room rewards. - **Punching down to survive**: getting cruel because you're rattled, and the room turns on you for it. Fix: the crowd forgives a clever hit, never a mean one — stay above the line.
The rule: a heckle is unscripted attention, and attention is the whole job. Don't defend the joke — absorb the interruption and make it part of the show. That's the beat that turns a rattled open-miker into someone the room decides to trust.

item.title: Soreness is not a scoreboard
item.description:
Two decades coaching lifters and the belief that will not die: that being wrecked the next day means the session worked. I've watched people chase the ache instead of the adaptation, adding volume purely to feel destroyed, then wondering why the numbers on the bar stopped moving. Soreness tells you a stimulus was novel. It does not tell you it was productive.
Named failure modes I've watched people pay for: - **The novelty tax**: switch every exercise every week to stay sore, and you never repeat a movement long enough to actually get better at it. You feel worked; you never get strong. Fix: keep your main lifts stable for weeks and let progress, not soreness, tell you it's working — more weight or more clean reps at the same effort. - **The recovery debt**: chasing next-day pain buries you so deep that sessions three and four of the week are garbage, so your weekly quality drops even as your suffering climbs. Fix: judge a program by what you can repeat on schedule, not by the worst you felt once. - **The ego-eccentric trap**: hammering slow negatives purely for the burn, wrecking connective tissue you can't feel until it's an injury. Fix: earn eccentric volume gradual

item.title: Motivation follows action — it does not lead it
item.description:
Twenty years sitting across from people waiting to "feel ready," and the most expensive myth in the room is that motivation is a precondition. People treat it like weather — something that arrives, that you wait out, that you can't start without. In practice the feeling of wanting-to almost always shows up AFTER the first small action, not before it. Waiting for it is waiting for a bus at the wrong stop.
Named patterns I've watched people pay for: - **The readiness trap**: postponing the task until the internal state is right, which guarantees the state never comes because the action that would produce it never happens. Fix: shrink the first step until it's too small to need motivation — two minutes, one page, one set — and let the doing generate the wanting. - **The mood-dependency loop**: tying whether you act to how you feel, so a bad morning becomes a lost day and the lost day becomes evidence you're the kind of person who can't. Fix: decouple action from mood by pre-committing to the behavior, not the feeling — you show up regardless, and the feeling catches up or it doesn't. - **The all-or-nothing reset**: deciding that if you can't do the full thing you'll do no

item.title: If you have to explain the joke, you already lost the room
item.description:
Twenty years of open mics and paid rooms and the tell I see in every new comic: the panic add-on. The joke lands soft, so they tack on "...you know what I mean?" or re-say the premise slower, as if the laugh was hiding behind comprehension. It wasn't. The room got it. It just didn't think it earned a laugh yet, and explaining is you arguing with them about it.
Named failure modes I've eaten on stage: - **The clarifier tag**: adding a line that restates the setup because you're scared they missed it. Now the real tag lands late, on a room that's already moved on. Fix: trust the premise landed; if it truly didn't, that's a writing problem to fix at home, not on stage. - **The over-signposted callback**: reminding the audience of the earlier bit before you call back to it — "remember when I said..." — which kills the whole pleasure of them connecting it themselves. Fix: callbacks work because the audience does the work; hand them the dots, never the line. - **The apology laugh-beg**: when a bit dies you explain why it was supposed to be funny, which is the single least funny thing a human can do into a microphone. item.description:
Twenty years in and the flag graveyard is real: I've inherited codebases where a third of the flags were "temporary" rollouts from three years ago, each one a live `if` branch that QA never covers and nobody dares delete. A flag is a promise to make a decision later. When later never comes, you're paying interest on a loan you forgot you took.
Named failure modes I've paid for: - **The permanent temporary**: a rollout flag defaulted on for everyone eighteen months ago, still wrapped in a conditional, still doubling the test matrix of every function it touches. Fix: every flag gets an expiry date and an owner at birth; a flag with no removal ticket doesn't merge. - **The zombie branch**: the "off" path bit-rotted because nobody exercised it, then a panic rollback flipped the flag and shipped code that hadn't compiled cleanly in a year. item.title: The joke gets the laugh — the tag gets the respect
item.description:
Twenty years of sets taught me new comics leave most of their laughs on the table by walking away the second a joke lands. The punchline opens the door; the tag is the three extra laughs waiting on the other side of it, free, if you don't bolt.
Scar tissue, catalogued: - **The premature exit**: you hit the punchline, the room laughs, and you immediately pivot to a new setup — killing the momentum you just bought. I've watched a killer bit get one laugh when it had four in it. Fix: sit in the premise, angle it again, tag it before you move on. - **The tag that resets instead of escalates**: a good tag heightens the same absurdity; a bad one starts a whole new thought and makes the room work again from cold. Fix: the tag rides the same wave — it doesn't build a new one. - **Tagging a joke that didn't land**: you can't tag silence. If the base joke died, the tag dies twice. Fix: only tag what killed.
The rule: the punchline is the sale, the tag is the upsell. Learn to stay in the moment one beat longer than feels safe — that beat is where the set separates from the open mic.

item.title: The best program is the one you can still run in week nine
item.description:
Two decades of coaching and the people who transform aren't the ones with the hardest week one — they're the ones with the most boring week thirty. Intensity is easy to summon once and impossible to bank. Consistency is what actually compounds.
Failure modes I see on repeat: - **The hero week**: someone trains six brutal days, gets crushed, and takes the next ten off recovering. Net stimulus: near zero, plus a soured relationship with training. I've watched this cycle burn out more beginners than any injury. Fix: pick a volume you could repeat if you were mildly tired — that's your real starting line, not your best day. - **Program hopping**: chasing the newest "optimal" split every three weeks means never running one long enough to adapt. The adaptation is in the repetition, not the design. - **All-or-nothing scheduling**: miss one session, write off the whole week. Fix: a short session beats a skipped one; showing up frequently matters more than the perfect dose.
Do this: design for your worst realistic week, not your best imagined one. A program you finish beats a better one you quit.

item.title: Certainty is a feeling — and feelings are terrible at fact-checking
item.description:
Two decades across the table from anxious, stuck people and the trap I see most often: they treat the *feeling* of certainty as if it were evidence. "I just know they're angry at me." "I'm sure this will go wrong." The conviction is real; the data is missing.
Failure modes I've watched play out: - **Emotional reasoning**: "I feel it strongly, so it must be true." The intensity of a belief has nothing to do with its accuracy — panic feels exactly as certain as insight. I've watched people torch relationships over a "certainty" that never had a fact under it. Fix: ask "what would I actually need to see to know this?" then go look. - **Confusing prediction with prophecy**: dreading an outcome so vividly it feels already decided, so you stop trying to change it. The certainty becomes self-fulfilling. Fix: treat the fear as one hypothesis, not the verdict. - **Closure-seeking**: the discomfort of not-knowing is so loud that any answer, even a bad one, feels like relief. So the mind grabs the fastest certainty available.
Do this: when you feel certain and it hurts, separate the feeling from the claim. The feeling is real. Whether the claim is true is a completely different

item.title: A retry without a cap is a DDoS you wrote against yourself
item.description:
Twenty years in and the outage that still makes me wince wasn't caused by the failing service — it was caused by everything downstream "helpfully" retrying it into the ground. The dependency blipped for two seconds; the retries kept it down for twenty minutes.
Named failure modes I've paid for: - **Synchronized retries**: every client retries on the same fixed interval, so the load arrives in perfect waves and the recovering service never gets a quiet window to stand up. I've watched a backend flap up-down-up because its own clients wouldn't let it breathe. Fix: full jitter on every backoff — randomize, never align. - **Retries with no ceiling**: "keep trying until it works" quietly means "keep trying after the user has already left." I've seen a queue fill with retries for requests nobody was waiting on anymore. Fix: cap attempts AND bind them to the request deadline. - **Retrying non-idempotent writes**: the first call actually succeeded, the response got lost, and the retry double-charged. Fix: idempotency keys on every write you'd retry.

item.title: A callback lands because the room remembers — not because your notes do
item.description:
Twenty years of sets taught me the callback is the most oversold move in comedy. New comics plant one because it looks clever on paper, then it dies because the room never actually held the first bit long enough to miss it.
Scar tissue, catalogued: - **The forced plant**: you set up a phrase early purely to call it back, but the setup itself didn't earn a laugh, so the callback references something nobody cared about. I've watched a room go silent at a callback to a line they'd already forgotten. Fix: only call back what actually killed — if the original didn't land, there's nothing to return to. - **Explaining the callback**: the second you gesture at "remember when I said…" you've killed it. The joy is the room getting there half a beat before you. Fix: trust the reference to be recognized; if you have to point at it, cut it. - **Callback too far downstream**: forty minutes of new material buries the original past recall. Timing isn't just within a bit, it's across the set. Fix: keep the loop tight enough that the memory is still warm.
The rule: a callback is a gift the room gives itself. Your job is to make the first bit worth remembering, then get out of the way

item.title: Rumination feels like problem-solving — that's exactly why it traps you
item.description:
Two decades sitting across from stuck people and the pattern I trust most: the ones who can't stop "thinking it through" are almost never solving anything. Rumination wears the costume of diligence, which is why it's so hard to put down — it feels responsible.
Failure modes I've watched play out: - **The problem with no next action**: real problem-solving ends in a step you can take. Rumination loops on questions with no lever — "why did I say that," "what if it goes wrong." I've watched people spend a week on a question that has no doable answer. Fix: ask "what's the next physical action?" If there isn't one, the thinking is the symptom, not the work. - **Mistaking rehearsal for control**: replaying a future conversation twenty times feels like preparation. It's anxiety buying the illusion of control over an outcome you don't own. Fix: prepare once, on paper, then close the loop deliberately. - **Analysis as avoidance**: staying in the head is safer than acting, so the mind generates "just one more consideration" forever. The thinking is the escape hatch from the doing.

item.title: Strength you can't reach isn't strength — it's a liability under load
item.description:
Two decades of coaching and the injuries I've watched happen most weren't from weak muscles — they were from strong muscles meeting a joint that had no room to move. People chase the number and quietly lose the range that keeps the number safe.
Failure modes I see on repeat: - **Half-rep creep**: the weight goes up because the range goes down, an inch at a time, until the "PR" is a quarter of the movement. I've seen a lifter add 40kg and lose the bottom of the squat entirely. Fix: pick a depth standard and never let load buy you a shorter rep. - **Passive flexibility with no strength in it**: someone can be pulled into a deep stretch but has zero control there, so the end range is a cliff, not a floor. That's where things tear. Fix: train strength AT the end range — pause reps, loaded stretches — so the position is owned, not just visited. - **Warmups that skip the joint you're about to load**: benching heavy off cold shoulders, pulling off a locked-up thoracic. The tissue isn't ready to reach where the bar demands.
Do this: audit your working depth monthly. If load is climbing while range is shrinking, you're not getting stronger — you're narrowing the window where

item.title: A cache you can't invalidate on demand is a bug with good latency
item.description:
Twenty years in and the outages that scared me most weren't the loud ones — they were the quiet stale reads. A cache makes the fast path fast and the wrong path invisible. Nobody pages you for "correct but two hours old." The user just quietly gets a lie.
Named failure modes I've paid for: - **The orphaned key**: we cached under one key shape, invalidated under another, and the two drifted the day someone renamed a field. Reads looked healthy; the data was fossil. Fix: derive the invalidation key from the exact same function that builds the read key — never hand-write it twice. - **TTL as a prayer**: "it'll expire in five minutes" is not a correctness strategy, it's a bet that nobody notices for five minutes. I've watched a pricing bug ride a TTL straight into a customer invoice. Fix: for anything money- or trust-shaped, invalidate on write, and treat TTL as a safety net, not the plan. - **Thundering herd on expiry**: everything expires at once, every request stampedes the origin, and the cache that was protecting the DB becomes the thing that kills it. Fix: jitter your TTLs and use a single-flight lock so one request refills while others wait.

item.title: Your opener is a promise, not a warmup
item.description:
Twenty years of rooms taught me the first ninety seconds set the contract for the whole set. New comics treat the opener as throat-clearing and burn the room's goodwill before they've made a case for why to listen. The open tells them who you are and how hard they can laugh.
Scar tissue, catalogued: - **Apologizing on the way in**: "I'm not really a comedian, but—" hands the room permission to doubt you, and they take it. I've watched a good set never recover from a soft first line. Fix: open on your most defensible bit, not your newest one. - **Front-loading context**: three minutes of setup before the first real laugh, and by then they've decided you're work, not fun. Fix: earn a laugh fast, then spend the credit on the longer runners. - **Misreading the room's temperature**: opening high-energy into a quiet late crowd, or low into a hot one, reads as tone-deaf. Match first, then lead.
The rule: the opener is a promise about the next twenty minutes. Make one you can keep, up front, with your strongest material.

item.title: Tempo is the load you've been hiding from
item.description:
Two decades coaching and the cheapest strength unlock I know isn't more plates — it's slowing the eccentric down until the lift stops lying to you. Bouncing and momentum let you move weight you never actually controlled, and the body only adapts to what it controls.
Failure modes I see on repeat: - **Bouncing out of the hole**: lifters use the stretch reflex to fling out of a squat or bench, then wonder why the middle of the range is weak. I've watched a "strong" lifter fold the moment tempo removed the bounce. Fix: a two-count lower on your main lift for a block; the weight drops and the honesty returns. - **Ego-loading the concentric**: chasing the number up while the lower half is freefall, which is where most people get hurt. Fix: own the descent first — control it and the injuries and the plateaus both ease. - **No pause where it counts**: touch-and-go hides positional weakness. A brief pause at the hardest point exposes exactly where you're bluffing.
Do this: pick one main lift and run a slow eccentric for four weeks. The load you can move honestly is the load that actually makes you stronger.

item.title: A boundary is about your behavior, not controlling theirs
item.description:
Two decades sitting with people taught me the most misunderstood word in the room is "boundary." People think it's a rule they impose on someone else's behavior. It isn't — it's a statement about what *you* will do, and it only works because it doesn't require the other person to cooperate.
Failure modes I've watched play out: - **The disguised demand**: "my boundary is you can't raise your voice at me" is not a boundary, it's a wish for control, and it collapses the second they do it anyway. I've watched people feel powerless because their "boundary" depended on someone else's compliance. Fix: "if voices get raised, I'll leave the room" — that one you can actually keep. - **Announcing without enforcing**: stating the line ten times and never acting on it teaches everyone the line is decorative. The follow-through is the boundary; the words are just a courtesy warning. - **Guilt as a veto**: feeling cruel for protecting your own limit, so you fold. The discomfort of holding it is the cost of having one.
Do this: phrase every boundary as your own action, then be willing to take it. The power is that it never needed their permission.

item.title: A rollback plan you've never actually run is a wish, not a plan
item.description:
Twenty years of deploys and the incident that still stings: we had a rollback "procedure" in the runbook, everyone signed off on it, and the night we needed it it took forty minutes to discover step 3 hadn't worked since a schema change six months earlier. A rollback you haven't executed under load is a hypothesis.
Named failure modes I've paid for: - **The one-way migration**: someone shipped a destructive schema change with no down-path, so "rolling back" the code left it pointed at a table that no longer matched. I've watched a team choose between two broken states at 2am. Fix: expand-and-contract — add columns, dual-write, backfill, and only drop the old shape a full deploy cycle later when rollback is still safe. - **Rollback that skips the cache**: we reverted the binary but the poisoned entries lived on in a warm cache, so the "rolled back" system kept serving the bug. Fix: rollback plans name every stateful layer, not just the artifact. - **Never rehearsed**: the plan was written once and never run, so nobody knew it had rotted. Fix: rehearse rollback in staging on a schedule, same as a fire drill.

item.title: Mobility is just strength you can actually reach
item.description:
Two decades of coaching and I've stopped calling it "flexibility." Flexibility is a party trick; mobility is control through a range you own under load. I've watched strong people with no usable range blow out a low back reaching for something dumb, because their strength lived in a tiny slice of motion and quit the second they left it.

item.title: Edit on your feet, not in your notebook
item.description:
Twenty years of open mics and late shows taught me the ugly truth: your notebook lies to you. A bit reads great at the kitchen table and dies on stage, and no amount of rewriting at home fixes it, because the audience is the only editor whose notes count. I've bombed with jokes I was certain were perfect on paper.
Named failure modes I've watched comics fall into: - **Notebook polishing**: rewriting a bit twelve times at home to "get it right" before ever trying it, then being shocked when the live crowd doesn't laugh at the version you fell in love with alone. I've wasted months this way. Fix: take the ugly first draft to a real room fast — the tag you need is usually something the crowd hands you, not something you'll ever invent at your desk. - **Ignoring where the laugh actually lands**: the joke gets a laugh but on a different word than you wrote, and you keep forcing your original beat. item.description:

item.description:

I've paid for that mistake in a weekend I don't get back.

item.title: Willpower is a design problem, not a character flaw
item.description:
Two decades sitting across from people who called themselves lazy, and I've almost never met a willpower problem that wasn't actually an environment problem wearing a guilt costume. The person isn't weak — the setup is asking them to spend a scarce resource on something a small design change could make free.
Named failure modes I've watched people blame themselves for: - **Relying on motivation to bridge friction**: they leave the hard thing three steps away and the easy distraction one tap away, then flog themselves for "choosing" wrong. I've seen people carry that shame for years. Fix: move the friction — make the good default one step closer and the bad one a step farther, and let geometry do the deciding. - **Confusing a feeling with a decision**: they wait to feel ready, treat the absence of the feeling as failure, and never start. item.description:

item.title: Idempotency is a contract, not a retry checkbox
item.description:
Twenty years in and I still see teams treat idempotency as a thing you sprinkle on a handler when the on-call gets paged. It isn't a feature you add — it's a contract you either honor at every layer or silently violate at the one that matters.
Named failure modes I've personally cleaned up at bad hours: - **The at-least-once lie**: a queue promises at-least-once delivery, and the team writes the consumer as if it were exactly-once. I've watched a payment worker double-charge because a broker redelivered on a rebalance and the handler had no dedupe key. item.title: The intensity you can't repeat next week doesn't count
item.description:
Two decades of coaching and the single biggest lie I've had to un-teach is that the hardest session is the best session. The body doesn't adapt to the effort you gave once — it adapts to the stimulus you can return to before the adaptation fades.
Named failure modes I've watched wreck otherwise disciplined people: - **The hero workout that costs a week**: someone empties the tank on a Monday, is too wrecked to train Wednesday or Friday, and nets fewer quality sessions than the person who never went to failure. I've seen this stall progress for months. Fix: leave two reps in reserve on most working sets so tomorrow is still on the table. - **Chasing soreness as the scoreboard**: they equate being wrecked with progress and keep manufacturing damage instead of adaptation. I've had clients plateau for a year doing this. item.title: Your cache is a second source of truth, and nobody agreed to that
item.description:
Twenty years of shipping and the nastiest data bugs I've chased almost never lived in the database. The moment a cache can return an answer the database wouldn't, you have two sources of truth and a race to decide which one lies today.

item.title: Adding load is not the same as making progress — I've watched people confuse them for years
item.description:
After two decades coaching, the lie that injures the most people isn't laziness — it's the belief that a heavier bar this week means you got stronger. Load is an input. Adaptation is the output. When you chase the input and ignore whether the body actually absorbed it, you're not training, you're just accumulating damage on credit.
Failure modes I see on repeat: - **Ego-linear progression**: adding weight every session because the spreadsheet says so, while bar speed craters and form drifts. I've watched a lifter "PR" a grind so ugly it cost them a month off. Fix: progress the quality of the rep before the number — clean and fast, then heavier. - **Volume as a virtue**: treating more sets as automatically better, until sleep and joints quietly foot the bill. Fix: the least volume that still drives adaptation is the winning dose, not the most you can survive. - **No deload story**: pushing hard with no planned backoff, so the "sudden" injury was actually months of ignored signal. item.description:
Twenty years on stage and the callbacks that land hardest were never in my notes. The room handed them to me. Comics fall in love with the *idea* of a callback — the clever button that ties the set in a bow — and force one in whether the room bought the setup or not. A callback to a bit that only half-landed isn't a payoff. It's you reminding everyone of the joke that didn't work.

Fix: only call back what got a real laugh — the size of the first laugh is the receipt. - **Over-tagging the callback**: hitting the same reference a third and fourth time, sanding it down to nothing. item.title: A boundary is a rule for your own behavior, not a demand on theirs
item.description:
Twenty years sitting with people and the single most misunderstood word in the room is "boundary". People announce boundaries as ultimatums — "you can't talk to me like that" — and then feel betrayed when the other person keeps doing exactly that. A boundary you can only keep if someone else cooperates was never a boundary. It was a wish with a stern voice.
Failure modes I've watched play out again and again: - **The boundary-as-control-move**: using the language to try to change someone else's behavior, then escalating when they don't comply. I've watched this turn a reasonable request into a power struggle nobody wins. Fix: state what *you* will do — "if the yelling starts, I'll leave the room" — an action fully inside your own control. - **The unenforced boundary**: naming the line and then never acting when it's crossed, which teaches everyone the line is decorative. Fix: the follow-through is the boundary; the sentence is just the announcement. - **Boundaries as punishment**: weaponizing distance to hurt rather than to protect. item.title: Sleep is the training — the gym is just the stimulus
item.description:
Two decades of coaching and the hardest sell is still this: you don't get stronger in the session, you get stronger in the recovery. The barbell is the request; sleep is where the body actually writes the change to disk.
Named failure modes I've personally watched: - **The volume-junkie plateau**: a lifter adds sets every week, sleeps six hours, and can't understand why they've stalled for months. I've seen the same person break the plateau by cutting a workout and adding an hour of sleep — zero new training, all new results. Fix: when progress stops, audit recovery before you add stress. - **The weekend-catchup myth**: crushing sleep Saturday to "make up" for a wrecked week. I've watched people ride this for years and stay perpetually under-recovered, because you can't bank sleep like it's a savings account. item.description:
Twenty years of stage time and here's the thing nobody wants to hear at the open mic: the room can smell who you're aiming at faster than you can. Point the joke at the wrong target and the silence isn't confusion — it's judgment.
Named failure modes I've personally bombed with: - **The cheap-shot down**: going after the easy, powerless target for a fast laugh. I've had a bit land, get the laugh, and still feel the room cool on me for the rest of the set — they laughed and then they didn't trust me. Fix: aim at power, at yourself, at the shared absurdity; never at the person who can't punch back. - **The vague-target whiff**: writing a bit so afraid to name anyone that the audience can't tell what it's about. item.description:
Twenty years in and I keep meeting teams who deleted their metrics budget because "we can just grep the logs." Then an incident hits and they're paying a fortune to scan terabytes to answer a question a cheap counter would have answered instantly.

item.title: Anxiety is a smoke alarm, not the fire — stop treating the beep as the emergency
item.description:
Two decades sitting across from anxious people and the reframe that moves the needle most is this: the feeling is a detector, not a verdict. A smoke alarm going off doesn't mean the house is burning — it means something asked for a look.
Named failure modes I've personally watched: - **The alarm-worship loop**: treating every spike of dread as proof that something is truly wrong, which cranks the sensitivity higher, which produces more spikes. I've watched people spend years amplifying the detector instead of checking the room. Fix: separate "I feel alarmed" from "there is a fire," out loud, every time. - **The avoidance discount**: dodging the trigger to make the beep stop, which works for an hour and teaches the alarm that the threat was real. item.description:
Twenty years sitting across from people who came in "just needing to vent," and the myth I fight most is catharsis: the idea that expressing anger drains it. Mostly it doesn't. Mostly it rehearses it. I've watched people talk themselves angrier in real time and call it processing.
Named failure modes I've seen up close: - **The loop-in disguise**: retelling the same grievance to a new audience, each retelling deepening the groove. Fix: the supportive move is one lap of validation, then a pivot to agency, not another lap. - **The identity glue**: telling the story so often the grievance becomes who you are. item.description:

item.description:
Two decades of training people and myself, and the belief that won't die is that a good session is measured by how wrecked you feel the next day. I've coached strong, patient people into needless plateaus because they optimized for pain instead of progress.
Named failure modes I've watched play out: - **The DOMS chase**: switching exercises constantly just to stay sore, which quietly guarantees you never add load to the same movement twice. item.title: The only real death on stage is explaining the joke
item.description:
I've bombed plenty of ways over the years, but the one that still makes me wince is the recovery-explain: the bit didn't land, so I told the room why it should have. That's not a save. That's an autopsy performed on a live patient.
Named failure modes I've earned the hard way: - **The nervous over-clarify**: adding "you know, because..." after a punchline that was already clear. I've watched myself sand the edge right off a good line because silence scared me. Fix: land it, shut up, let the pause do the work — trust I built the setup. - **The apology tag**: following a soft laugh with "that one's new" or "sorry." I've done it on stage and felt the room stop rooting for me the instant I stopped rooting for the bit. Fix: never editorialize your own material mid-set; move. - **The rescue explanation**: when a joke dies, resurrecting it by dissecting it. I've turned one dead bit into three by explaining the first. Fix: bury it, hard-cut to the next premise, and let momentum reset the room.

item.title: Rest days are training days your ego doesn't log
item.description:
I've spent twenty years coaching people who treat rest like theft — like every day off the gym floor is progress leaking out of them. item.description:

item.description:

item.description:
I've watched clients spend years announcing boundaries the way people announce diets — loudly, once, and with no plan for Thursday. Twenty years of sitting across from burned-out people has taught me the boundary was never the hard part. The upkeep is.
Named failure modes I've watched people pay for:

item.description:

They train seven days deep, plateau, get hurt, and call it bad luck. It wasn't luck. The adaptation they were chasing happens between sessions, and they never let it.
Failure modes I see on repeat: - **The stolen rest day**: "just a light session" that drifts into a real one, every single week. I've watched lifters undercut a whole training block this way and blame the program. Fix: schedule recovery like a workout, with a plan — walk, mobility, sleep — and defend it. - **Confusing soreness with progress**: chasing the wrecked feeling as proof it worked, so every week is a demolition and nothing gets rebuilt. Fix: judge sessions by performance trend over weeks, not by how broken you feel the next morning. - **Recovering the body, ignoring the sleep**: perfect deload week, five hours of sleep a night. Fix: the deload's first assignment is bedtime — nothing else on the recovery menu outranks it.

item.title: Avoidance is a loan with interest paid in dread
item.description:
Two decades across the table and the most expensive habit I treat isn't dramatic — it's the quiet one. The unopened letter. The unanswered message. The appointment not booked. Avoidance works instantly, which is exactly why it's dangerous: the relief is real, and it teaches your brain that the thing was worth avoiding.
Failure modes I've watched play out: - **The relief trap**: dodge the task, feel better for an hour, and the anxiety returns bigger because now there's evidence the thing is scary. I've watched a two-minute email grow into a three-month dread that ran someone's whole autumn. Fix: name the pattern out loud — "this is avoidance paying out" — the label alone loosens its grip. - **Waiting to feel ready**: postponing until the fear passes, when action is the only thing that makes it pass. Fix: reverse the order — do a five-minute version first; readiness is a result, not a prerequisite. - **The invisible pile**: each avoided item is small, so none of them counts, until the pile itself becomes the thing being avoided. item.description:
Twenty years of on-call and the worst incidents I've worked were never silent — they were announced, loudly, into a channel everyone had muted. The alert fired. Nobody moved. We had trained ourselves, one false alarm at a time, to hear noise instead of signal.
Named failure modes I've paid for: - **The always-red dashboard**: a wall of warnings that has been red so long it's the background color. I've watched a genuine disk-full page sit forty minutes because it looked exactly like the four hundred fake ones before it. Fix: an alert that doesn't demand an action gets deleted or demoted — no third state. - **Threshold set once, never revisited**: traffic tripled, the alert threshold didn't, and now it fires nightly at peak like clockwork. Fix: every recurring alert gets a review — tune it, fix the cause, or kill it. Recurrence is a bug in the alert, not weather. - **Alerting on causes instead of symptoms**: paging on CPU instead of latency, so you wake up for a busy-but-healthy box and sleep through a slow-but-idle one. Fix: page on what the user feels; graph the rest.

item.title: The opener buys permission, not applause
item.description:
Twenty years of rooms — clubs, corporates, back-of-a-bar Tuesdays — and the hardest lesson to teach a newer comic is what the first thirty seconds are actually *for*. It's not for your best joke. It's for answering the only question the audience is silently asking: "are we safe with this person?" I've bombed with killer material because I spent the open proving I was clever instead of proving I was in control.
Named failure modes I've eaten on stage:
- **The A-bomb open.** Leading with your closer-grade joke. If it hits, everything after feels like a decline. If it misses, you've spent your credibility and your best bullet in the same breath. - **The apology walk-on.** Opening with "I just wrote this" or "bear with me." You've told the room not to trust you before they had a chance to. I've watched comics negotiate themselves out of a laugh they'd already earned. - **The borrowed energy.** Coming out at the headliner's pace when you're the opener at eight percent room warmth.
